final_answer:
Bottom line: Yes, there is recourse, but it runs on two tracks, and the immigration-court track must come first. (1) In immigration court, file a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia removal order on the ground of lack of notice, under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii). That motion may be filed at any time, so April 2026 is not late, and filing it automatically stays removal. If it is granted, the proceedings are reopened and the husband can renew his I-485 before the IJ. (2) With USCIS, file a motion to reopen/reconsider (Form I-290B) the I-130 abandonment denial and the I-485 denial.

WHAT TO FILE WITH THE IMMIGRATION COURT. File a written motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order with the immigration court that entered it, using the Immigration Court Practice Manual format. This can be done through ECAS or on paper, and the motion should be served on DHS/ICE OPLA. The grounds are that (a) the husband did not receive notice of the hearing, and (b) alternatively, if he can show them, exceptional circumstances. Exceptional circumstances carry a 180-day deadline, which has passed, so lack of notice is the vehicle. The motion should include: a sworn declaration from the husband that he never received the NTA or hearing notice and was unaware of the case; his address history and the address he actually gave USCIS (the I-130/I-485 filings); proof that the NTA and RFE were mailed to an address he never provided; and a statement that he did not know of the order until April 1, 2026. It should also include the Form EOIR-33 change-of-address form (filed with the motion or before it), a copy of the removal order, and the relief he will seek if reopened. That relief is renewal of the I-485 adjustment of status based on the I-130, plus a request that the IJ adjudicate or continue for the I-130. Include a copy of the I-485/I-130 and evidence of the bona fide marriage, since adjustment is a form of relief. Request a stay of removal even though the stay is automatic. Notice-based reopening requires that notice was not properly provided. Under Campos-Chaves v. Garland (2024), a person who received a proper notice of the hearing he missed cannot rescind on notice grounds even if the NTA was defective. Under Niz-Chavez, an NTA must be a single document. Here the husband's claim is that notice went to an address he never provided. Because INA 239(a)(2) and (c) rely on the address the noncitizen provided, mailing to an address he never provided, with no evidence he gave it, supports non-receipt and non-compliance. Caveat: if the NTA was served in person or the address came from him in some record, the analysis changes. The motion should obtain and attach the record of proceedings and any address DHS relied on.

FEES. Based on secondary sources (not verified against the primary EOIR fee page, which I could not access), there is no fee for a motion to reopen an in absentia order based on lack of notice under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii). Ordinary motions to reopen cost $145 plus the $900 H.R.1 (2025) fee, and the H.R.1 fee is not waivable. Under the secondary-source summary, the lack-of-notice motion is exempt. Counsel should confirm with the current EOIR fee schedule (8 CFR 1103.7 and EOIR guidance) as of April 2026 before filing. If a fee is required, EOIR fees are paid to DHS, not to the court, and the receipt is filed with the motion. A fee waiver request (EOIR-26A style) is available for the base fee but not the H.R.1 fee.

USCIS TRACK. The I-130 denial for failure to respond to the RFE is an abandonment denial. Under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15) it cannot be appealed, but a motion to reopen under 8 CFR 103.5 is available, and it requires evidence that the RFE was sent to an address other than the one on the filing. That fits these facts. The usual deadline is 30 days (33 by mail) from the decision, which has long passed; 103.5 permits USCIS discretion to excuse delay only where it was reasonable and beyond the control of the applicant, and the mailing error helps. The I-485 denial, which presumably followed the I-130 denial, can be challenged by an I-290B motion, but the stronger route is renewal in removal proceedings. Under 8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)(ii), a non-arriving noncitizen may renew an adjustment application denied by USCIS before the IJ. He is not an arriving alien, as he was admitted on a B-2 visa. As an immediate relative of a US citizen, he is exempt from 245(c)(2) overstay bars, and his admission supports 245(a) eligibility; the unapproved I-130 is a problem, but the IJ can adjudicate the I-130 in practice only if DHS/USCIS has it (the IJ has no jurisdiction over the I-130 itself), so a USCIS motion to reopen the I-130 is needed in parallel. Do not rely on denials being treated as pending; the denials were final.

Risks and open points: the Board/circuit law on what suffices to prove non-receipt; whether DHS used the address of record; whether the removal order has led to ICE enforcement (the automatic stay is only while the motion is pending, and you should ask for a stay); and possible federal-court review in the circuit. Seek counsel promptly.
